discovery: Optical detection and coherent control of single electron spins in diamond (NV centres) and their development into quantum sensors
motivation: Wrachtrup and Jelezko first detected the magnetic resonance of a single nitrogen-vacancy spin in diamond by optical means and then controlled it coherently at room temperature. Before that, single-spin control had needed cryogenic or ultra-high-vacuum isolation. Lukin, with Wrachtrup and Walsworth's teams, showed that this isolated quantum system could serve as a nanoscale magnetometer with atomic-scale spatial resolution. As a result, one spin, read out with photons, became a practical metrological instrument. NV sensors now image magnetism in two-dimensional materials and superconductors, detect nuclear magnetic resonance from nanolitre volumes, measure fields inside living cells and work inside diamond anvil cells beyond 100 GPa. The work joins foundational quantum control to a new, reliable measurement capability across condensed-matter physics, biology and geoscience. It extends the tradition of Nobel-recognised single-quantum-system experiments into widely used quantum technology.
